name: why arrays are faster than they look
hook: arr[7] doesn't search for index 7. It computes where it is. That one fact explains what arrays are good and bad at.
hook_slide: `arr[7]` doesn't search for index 7. *It computes where it is.*
hook_sub: Why arrays are faster than they look.
caption: An array is one contiguous block of memory holding equal-sized slots. So the address of slot i is pure arithmetic: base + i × slot size. Base {base}, {slot}-byte slots: index {i} lives at {addr}. No searching, O(1).
The price of being packed: no gaps allowed. Insert at the front and everything shifts. {n} front inserts cost {front_writes} writes; {n} appends cost {end_writes}.
The hidden bonus: CPUs fetch a {line}-byte cache line at a time, which holds {per_line} four-byte integers. Read one and the next {free_reads} are already in cache.
When two designs tie on paper, bet on the contiguous one.
Ever shipped a loop of front-inserts? 👇
cta: Then build a dynamic array from scratch in the next lesson.

p: Because the slots are equal-sized and packed, the address of slot i is pure arithmetic.
No other position is touched. That is why `arr[i]` is O(1).
Insert at the front and every element shifts one slot. It reads as one line and moves the entire array.
The triangular sum, n(n+1)/2: one of the most common accidental quadratics in real code.
CPUs pull a cache line at a time, typically {line} bytes: {per_line} four-byte integers.
Read `arr[0]` and the next {free_reads} reads hit cache for free, about {hit_pct}%. When two designs tie on paper, bet on the contiguous one.
